title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context. Euler is setting up the planar dynamics of a thin rod or string with arclength s and time t. Φ(s,t) is the angle of the tangent, with dx/ds = sinΦ and dy/ds = cosΦ, so Φ is measured from the y-axis. The other quantities are:
- T: tension along the tangent.
- V: normal (shear) force.
- Vv: bending moment.
- S(s): absolute elasticity, i.e. flexural rigidity, a function of s only.
- Σ: the thickness (mass per length); Σ/2g is mass density in Euler's units, with g the fall in one second.
- P, Q: applied elementary forces.

The four equations on the previous page are:
- (I) tangential force balance.
- (II) normal force balance.
- (III) the moment–curvature law Vv = S ∂Φ/∂s.
- (IV) moment balance ∂(Vv)/∂s = V, which neglects rotatory inertia.

§XLI (end). Eliminating the lever arm v between III and IV gives V = ∂/∂s(S Φ_s) = S Φ_ss + S' Φ_s, so the shear force is the derivative of the bending moment. Substituting this into I and II leaves two equations in T and Φ. Eliminating T then yields one 'final principal' PDE for Φ(s,t); x and y follow by quadrature from x_s = sinΦ, y_s = cosΦ.

§XLII. Euler remarks that beyond infinitely small oscillations almost nothing is known, and no method exists for the intricate nonlinear equations. He therefore recovers the classical vibrating-string equation as a check:
- Perfect flexibility gives V = 0 and P = Q = 0.
- Small transverse displacement y gives y_s ≈ 0, x_s ≈ 1, Φ ≈ π/2.
- The equations become T_s = (Σ/2g)(x_tt sinΦ + y_tt cosΦ) and T Φ_s = (Σ/2g)(x_tt cosΦ − y_tt sinΦ).

The sign in II follows correctly from the previous page's equation II with V = P = Q = 0. On the next page, x_tt = 0 and cosΦ = 0 give T constant. Then Φ_s = −y_ss gives T y_ss = (Σ/2g) y_tt, the d'Alembert/Euler string equation. §XLIII goes on to the beam (Euler–Bernoulli) case.
errors: Linearization is handled loosely. Euler sets dy/ds = 0 and cosΦ = 0 on this page, yet on the next page he differentiates cosΦ = dy/ds to get Φ_s = −y_ss. This is consistent only if y_s is treated as first-order small rather than zero; it is a standard informal step, not a real error.
Moment balance (IV) omits rotatory inertia, so the 'general' equations are not fully general (the rotary inertia term later added by Rayleigh). This is an approximation rather than a mistake.

ideas.what: Shear force equals derivative of bending moment, V = (S Φ_s)_s, from the moment–curvature law plus moment balance
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Bernoulli moment-shear relation / special Cosserat (Kirchhoff) rod equations in the plane
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E410, as analysed by Truesdell); James and Daniel Bernoulli for the moment–curvature law
ideas.where_published: E410 itself (Novi Comm. Acad. Petrop. 15, 1771); discussed in Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies 1638–1788 (Opera omnia II 11/2)

ideas.what: Reduction of the full nonlinear planar rod equations to a single PDE for the tangent angle Φ(s,t), after eliminating T
ideas.modern_name: Intrinsic (angle) formulation of the elastica / dynamic elastica

ideas.what: Recovery of the linear string equation as a small-amplitude, perfectly flexible special case
ideas.modern_name: Linearized wave equation for a string
ideas.where_published: E119, E140 and others; here as a consistency check

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a standard derivation (V = (SΦ_s)_s) followed by a routine linear limit to the string equation. E410's general rod equations, and Euler's remark that nonlinear motions are untreated, are well documented by Truesdell. Nothing here appears absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: 'motum cordatum vibrantium' is almost certainly 'motum chordarum (cordarum) vibrantium', vibrating strings.
Previous page, equation III: '(Vv=S(dΦ/dt)' should read Vv = S(dΦ/ds).
Previous page: 'functionem esse ipsius S tantum' should read 'ipsius s tantum' (lowercase arclength s).
